issues.description: check_process_exited fallback removed; reader can hang if writer exits without EOF on macOS
issues.detail: The prior code handled a macOS quirk: on some systems an empty read after the writer closes does not produce EOF or BlockingIOError. The new code deletes that guard (the `if content and check_process_exited(command_obj): break` branch) and replaces it with `pass`. If the FIFO never reaches the blocking-read path (e.g., writer closes before any data is sent, or the timeout fires before first read), the loop will spin forever or hang. The macOS comment was load-bearing; removing it without evidence the platform behavior changed is too clever by half.

issues.description: Two read loops where one data structure would do; the shape of the code is fighting the shape of the data
issues.detail: The fix introduces a second nested `while True: os.read` loop inside the outer poll loop, and the outer loop becomes mostly dead code once data arrives. Data here is a stream of bytes terminated by writer-close. The right shape is one read loop in one mode, not two loops that hand off via an fcntl flip. Consider: poll once for readability (or first byte), then drop into a single blocking drain loop and return. The current code reads like two algorithms stitched together.

issues.description: Mode switch via fcntl mid-read is clever; the simpler design opens the FIFO blocking from the start
issues.detail: The whole non-blocking-then-flip-to-blocking dance exists to keep `select.poll` for early failure detection. But a blocking read on a FIFO with a separate watchdog (timeout on the subprocess, or poll on a self-pipe / signalfd) is the standard Unix idiom and avoids fcntl gymnastics on a live fd. The current solution mixes two regimes on one descriptor; that is exactly the kind of cleverness Rule 4 warns about: harder to reason about, harder to debug if it ever misbehaves under load.

issues.description: BlockingIOError handler silently swallows the case; lost the prior signal that the file was closed
issues.detail: Old code treated BlockingIOError with content as `file was closed -> break`. New code just `pass`es. Combined with the removed process-exit check, the reader has fewer ways to notice the writer is gone. If the blocking-mode path is never entered, there is no termination condition other than the outer timeout. Worth being explicit about why this is safe now, or restoring a guarded break.

issues.description: Inline comment promises a POSIX guarantee that only holds for the blocking-drain path
issues.detail: The comment says blocking read returns 0 only after writer closes AND buffers drain — true, but only inside the inner loop, and only after the first non-empty read has occurred. If the writer never produces output (error path), the code never enters the inner loop and the POSIX guarantee does not apply. The comment overstates the safety of the overall function. Trim the claim to what is actually guaranteed.

issues.description: No test for the race being fixed
issues.detail: A truncation race at ~86KB is exactly the kind of bug that returns if someone rewrites this function later. A small unit test that writes >64KB to a FIFO and closes the writer abruptly (or uses a fork with `os._exit`) would lock in the fix. Without it, the next refactor will not know which invariant is load-bearing.

review.summary: The diagnosis is right: non-blocking reads on a FIFO can race with writer close and return short data while kernel buffers still hold bytes. The fix — drop into blocking mode once data arrives — works, but the code shape is fighting the data shape: two loops, an fcntl flip mid-stream, and a silently-removed macOS fallback. Data here is a single byte stream terminated by writer-close; the obvious design is one blocking drain loop with an external watchdog for the early-failure case. Decision label: TOO-CLEVER, leaning COULD-BE-A-FILTER. Restore (or justify removing) the macOS process-exit fallback, tighten the POSIX-guarantee comment to the inner loop only, and add a regression test that reproduces the >64KB truncation race.
